back: A well-defined collection of objects — we can definitely decide whether a given object belongs to the collection or not. E.g., rivers of India; NOT 'five most renowned mathematicians'.
Roster: list all elements in braces, e.g. {2, 4, 6}. Set-builder: state the common property, e.g. {x : x is an even positive integer less than 7}.

front: Symbols ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, ℝ stand for?
back: ℕ naturals {1,2,3,...}, ℤ integers {...,-1,0,1,...}, ℚ rationals p/q, ℝ reals. Superscript + means positive elements only.
∈ = 'belongs to / is an element of'; ∉ = 'does not belong to'. E.g., if V is the vowels, a ∈ V but b ∉ V.
(1) Order of listing doesn't matter. (2) Elements are never repeated — letters of SCHOOL = {S, C, H, O, L}.
'The set of all x such that x has property P.' Braces = 'the set of all', colon = 'such that'.
A set containing no element, denoted φ or { }. Example: {x : 1 < x < 2, x ∈ N}. Definition 1.
Finite: empty or has a definite number of elements (n(S) a natural number). Infinite: otherwise. Points on a line = infinite; days of week = finite. Definition 2.
The number of DISTINCT elements of S. If n(S) is a natural number, S is non-empty finite.
When they have exactly the same elements (A = B). Repetition and order don't matter: {1,2,3} = {2,2,1,3,3}. Definition 3.
A ⊂ B if every element of A is also an element of B: a ∈ A ⇒ a ∈ B. If A ⊂ B and A ≠ B, A is a PROPER subset.
A ⊂ B AND B ⊂ A ⇔ A = B (⇔ means 'if and only if').

front: Which set is a subset of every set?
back: The empty set φ (by agreement), since it has no element that could fail to be in the other set. Also every set is a subset of itself.
A set with exactly one element, e.g. {a}. Note {a} ≠ a.
N ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R; also T (irrationals) ⊂ R and N ⊄ T.
T = {x : x ∈ R and x ∉ Q} — all real numbers that are not rational. Members include √2, √5, π.
{y : a < y < b} — all points strictly between a and b; end points EXCLUDED.
{x : a ≤ x ≤ b} — end points INCLUDED.
[a,b) = {x : a ≤ x < b}: includes a, excludes b. (a,b] = {x : a < x ≤ b}: excludes a, includes b.
b − a for ALL four types — inclusion of end points doesn't change length.
The basic set relevant to a particular context; all sets under study are its subsets. E.g., ℕ when studying primes.
Named after John Venn (1834–1883). Universal set = rectangle; subsets = circles inside it; elements written in their circles.
{x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B} — all elements in either set, common ones taken once.
{x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B} — only the common elements.
Sets with NO common elements: A ∩ B = φ. Example: evens {2,4,6,8} and odds {1,3,5,7}.

front: If B ⊂ A, then A ∪ B = ?
back: A itself (union with a subset changes nothing). Similarly A ∩ B = B.
A∪B = B∪A; A∩B = B∩A. (A∪B)∪C = A∪(B∪C); (A∩B)∩C = A∩(B∩C).
A ∪ φ = A (φ identity of ∪); U ∩ A = A (U identity of ∩); A ∪ A = A and A ∩ A = A (idempotent).
A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C) — intersection distributes over union (and symmetrically union over intersection).
{x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B} — elements of A not in B. Note A – B ≠ B – A in general.

front: Mutually disjoint regions of two circles
back: A – B, A ∩ B, B – A are pairwise disjoint — their intersections are all φ (Fig 1.9).
{x : x ∈ U and x ∉ A} = U – A — elements of the universal set not in A. Then (A′)′ = A.
(A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′. Complement flips unions into intersections and vice versa.
A ∪ A′ = U, A ∩ A′ = φ, φ′ = U, U′ = φ.

front: Who founded set theory? Russell's Paradox?
back: Georg Cantor (1845–1918), via trigonometric series work (papers 1874–1897). Bertrand Russell (1902) showed 'set of all sets' leads to contradiction.
